item.title: DSIR 0.10.0: keep the detail behind health indicators
item.dc:creator: Shanlong Ding
item.description:
The first DSIR post introduced a shared format for WHO GHO and UN SDG data. DSIR 0.10.0 adds ways to inspect and keep the detail behind each observation: population breakdowns, units, sources, and notes. Both cleaners still return the same 15 columns by default.

These examples require DSIR 0.10.0 or later and dplyr. See the public repository for installation instructions. The first two examples call the live UN SDG API; the displayed results were retrieved on 4 October 2026.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(DSIR))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

stopifnot(packageVersion("DSIR") >= "0.10.0")

1. Look up official dimension codes

sdg_dimensions() reads series-specific code lists without downloading observations. include_attributes = TRUE also includes attributes such as units and data nature. Here we inspect age and sex codes for the SDG 3.8.2 series used below.

codebook <- suppressMessages(sdg_dimensions(
  "3.8.2", series = "SH_OOP_XPD_EARNNET40",
  include_attributes = TRUE
))
stopifnot(nrow(codebook) > 0L)

codebook %>%
  filter(kind == "dimension", dimension %in% c("Age", "Sex")) %>%
  select(dimension, code, label, sdmx) %>%
  head(8L)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  dimension code    label                              sdmx  
  <chr>     <chr>   <chr>                              <chr> 
1 Age       0-59    under 59 years old                 Y0T59 
2 Age       60+     60 years old and over              Y_GE60
3 Age       ALLAGE  All age ranges or no breaks by age _T    
4 Sex       BOTHSEX Both sexes                         _T    
5 Sex       FEMALE  Female                             F     
6 Sex       MALE    Male                               M

Use code in filters: the alternative sdmx representation can differ. A category in the codebook does not guarantee observations for every country.

2. Select a stratum and retain its context

This follows the documented national-total example for the Philippines. Dimension names and codes are exact and case-sensitive.

national.raw <- suppressMessages(sdg_data(
  "3.8.2", area = "PHL",
  series = "SH_OOP_XPD_EARNNET40",
  dimensions = list(
    Age = "ALLAGE", Location = "ALLAREA", Sex = "BOTHSEX",
    Quantile = "_T", Type_of_household = "_T"
  )
))
stopifnot(nrow(national.raw) > 0L)

national <- sdg_clean(
  national.raw, keep_dimensions = TRUE, keep_metadata = TRUE
)

national %>%
  select(iso3, year, value_num, dim_sex, attr_units, attr_nature) %>%
  tail(5L)
# A tibble: 5 × 6
  iso3   year value_num dim_sex attr_units attr_nature
  <chr> <int>     <dbl> <chr>   <chr>      <chr>      
1 PHL    2012      36.8 BOTHSEX PERCENT    G          
2 PHL    2015      35.2 BOTHSEX PERCENT    G          
3 PHL    2018      31.6 BOTHSEX PERCENT    C          
4 PHL    2021      33.8 BOTHSEX PERCENT    C          
5 PHL    2023      31.0 BOTHSEX PERCENT    C

keep_dimensions = TRUE appends named SDG columns such as dim_age and dim_sex; dim1 through dim3 remain GHO-only positions. keep_metadata = TRUE retains observation attributes, source and time context, and all footnotes and linked codes. Notes and linked codes are list-columns. See sdg_clean().

The filters run locally after all pages are downloaded. They do not reduce the number of pages fetched. DSIR checks declared page numbers, page counts, and total row counts before filtering. An inconsistent or incomplete download warns and returns no rows; counts omitted by the API cannot be verified. A requested dimension absent from the response also warns and returns no rows. sdg_coverage() accepts the same filters and now retains download warnings.

3. Save the result for reuse

snapshot(), added in 0.9.0, saves an expression’s result as an RDS file. RDS preserves the list-columns above. The second call proves that an existing snapshot is read without evaluating the expression again.

snapshot.path <- file.path(tempdir(), "sdg-3-8-2-phl-national.rds")
saved <- suppressMessages(snapshot(national, file = snapshot.path))
reused <- suppressMessages(snapshot(
  stop("This expression should not run."), file = snapshot.path
))
identical(saved, reused)
[1] TRUE

For reuse across R sessions, choose a fixed path in your project instead of tempdir(). refresh = TRUE re-evaluates the expression; put an API pull inside that expression when a refresh should download data again. An empty refresh is never written over a good snapshot; the older result is returned with a warning.

Other changes worth knowing

For GHO, gho_clean() can now retain each row’s dimension types (dim1_type through dim3_type), identifiers, source codes, time context, update timestamps, and comments. Types are copied from source fields rather than inferred from codes. bind_indicators() now preserves extra columns and fills missing fields when inputs have different dimensions.

Version 0.9.0 also added age_standardize() for direct age standardization with optional Fay-Feuer gamma confidence intervals, and life_table() for period life tables from age-specific mortality rates. The release notes describe the full changes.

item.title: One tidy workflow for WHO GHO and UN SDG data in R: introducing DSIR
item.dc:creator: Shanlong Ding
item.description:
If you have ever pulled indicator data from both the WHO Global Health Observatory (GHO) and the UN SDG database in the same project, you know the small frictions add up. The two APIs speak different dialects: GHO keys countries by ISO3 codes, the SDG API by UN M49 numeric codes. Their responses come back with different column names and different shapes. So before you can do any actual analysis, you end up writing — and rewriting — the same glue code to align them.

DSIR (“Data Science Infrastructure for Global Health”) is a small R package I wrote to take that friction away. It bundles country metadata, lightweight clients for the GHO and SDG APIs that return a single shared schema, and a set of WHO-style ggplot2 and flextable themes so the output already looks like something you can drop into a report.

It is on CRAN:

install.packages("DSIR")

Country metadata you don’t have to maintain

A surprising amount of global-health code starts by hand-maintaining a list of countries, regions, and ISO codes. DSIR ships that as data. who_countries is a tibble of all 194 WHO Member States, with ISO3 / ISO2 / UN M49 codes, official and short names, WHO region, and a flag for Pacific Island Countries:

library(DSIR)
library(dplyr)

who_countries |>
  filter(who_region == "WPR") |>
  select(iso3, name_short, is_pic)
# A tibble: 28 × 3
   iso3  name_short        is_pic
   <chr> <chr>             <lgl> 
 1 AUS   Australia         FALSE 
 2 BRN   Brunei Darussalam FALSE 
 3 KHM   Cambodia          FALSE 
 4 CHN   China             FALSE 
 5 COK   Cook Islands      TRUE  
 6 FJI   Fiji              TRUE  
 7 IDN   Indonesia         FALSE 
 8 JPN   Japan             FALSE 
 9 KIR   Kiribati          TRUE  
10 LAO   Lao PDR           FALSE 
# ℹ 18 more rows

There are also ready-made ISO3 vectors for each region — wpro_cty, afro_cty, euro_cty, and so on — that you can pass straight into the data functions. No more pasting country lists between scripts.

A consistent “search → fetch → clean” rhythm

Both API clients follow the same three-step rhythm, so once you’ve learned one you’ve learned both.

For GHO, you can search for an indicator, check coverage before committing to a download, then fetch and tidy:

# Search indicators by keyword
gho_indicators("mortality")

# Fetch premature NCD mortality for the Western Pacific, then tidy
raw <- gho_data("NCDMORT3070", spatial_type = "country", area = wpro_cty)
gho_clean(raw)

The SDG client works exactly the same way — and crucially, its area argument also accepts ISO3 codes, converting to M49 internally, so the same regional vectors just work:

# 3.4.1 = NCD mortality; pass ISO3 codes directly
raw <- sdg_data("3.4.1", area = wpro_cty)
sdg_clean(raw)

The payoff: one schema, so you can just stack them

Here is the part that saves the most time. gho_clean() and sdg_clean() both return the same 15-column schema (source, id, indicator, location, iso3, year, value, value_num, …). Because the shape is identical, GHO and SDG output combine directly — no manual renaming, no reconciling code systems:

gho <- gho_data("NCDMORT3070", area = wpro_cty) |> gho_clean()
sdg <- sdg_data("3.4.1",        area = wpro_cty) |> sdg_clean()

bind_indicators(gho, sdg)   # keep track of origin via the `source` column

That source column means you never lose track of where a row came from, even after you’ve stacked half a dozen indicators from both APIs.

Charts and tables that already look like WHO

The other recurring cost in this kind of work is making every chart and table look consistent across a report. DSIR includes publication-ready themes so you don’t restyle from scratch each time. Here theme_dsi() and scale_y_dsi_col() (which removes the gap between bars and the axis) do the work:

library(ggplot2)

who_countries |>
  count(who_region) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(who_region, n), n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0093D5") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_dsi_col() +
  theme_dsi() +
  labs(title = "WHO Member States by region", x = NULL, y = NULL)

For multi-panel layouts there’s theme_dsi_facet(), and for tables dsi_flextable_defaults() sets booktabs styling, bold headers and sensible padding in one line. The point is that a chart pulled straight from who_countries or a cleaned indicator already carries a consistent WHO look, without per-plot fiddling.

Try it

DSIR is on CRAN and the source is on GitHub:

install.packages("DSIR")
  • Documentation and a fuller walkthrough: https://shanlong-who.github.io/DSIR/
  • Source, issues, and feature requests: https://github.com/shanlong-who/DSIR/

It’s early days and the package is small by design — it does the unglamorous data-plumbing so the analysis can start sooner. If you work with WHO or SDG data in R and find it useful, I’d love to hear what’s missing; issues and suggestions are very welcome. And if it saves you some glue code, a GitHub star helps other people working on global health find it too.
